html:
The trans-Saharan trade was the caravan trade across the Sahara between North Africa and the Sahel, the grassland belt along the desert's southern edge. It began in ancient times, became regular once camels were widely used, and was at its height from the 8th century to the early 17th.

The Sahara had dried into a desert after about 3000 BCE and cut West Africa off from the Mediterranean. Crossing it only paid for goods of great value. The camel, which can go days without water, made regular crossings possible. Berber guides who knew the routes and wells led the caravans, which could number a thousand camels or more.

What moved:

  • South: salt, mined in desert pits such as Taghaza, along with horses, cloth, copper, glass and books.
  • North: gold from the Bambuk and Bure fields, ivory, kola nuts, and enslaved people, many of them women taken to North Africa and the Middle East.

The trade built empires in the Sahel. Ghana grew rich taxing gold and salt; then the Mali Empire, whose king Mansa Musa crossed the desert to Mecca in 1324 with so much gold that he became famous in Cairo and Europe; then the Songhai Empire. Further east, Kanem-Bornu ran its own route north to Libya.

Islam came with the merchants. Rulers and traders converted, and towns like Timbuktu became centres of scholarship. The traveller Ibn Battuta crossed with a caravan in 1352. The Berber Almoravids rose from the desert routes in the 11th century.

The trade declined after Portuguese ships reached the West African coast in the 15th century and drew gold toward the Atlantic. A Moroccan army crossed the desert and broke Songhai at the Battle of Tondibi in 1591, using guns. Smaller caravans kept crossing into the 20th century.
